This Mexican president founded the party that would dominate the country for decades, then ruled as de facto leader during a period called the Maximato. Who was he?
Plutarco Elías Calles: President of Mexico from 1924 to 1928.

Known as Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Ge'ez, this Hebrew Bible figure brought a caravan of lavish gifts to King Solomon and is linked by modern historians to an ancient South Arabian kingdom in Yemen?
Queen of Sheba: Historical figure in the Abrahamic religions.
A central tenet of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, this idea holds that an immortal soul never disperses at death but passes into a newborn baby or an animal. What's the concept?
Reincarnation: Concept of rebirth in different physical form.
Notorious for humiliating defendants and handing down frequent death sentences, this German judge presided over the People's Court from 1942 to 1945 — who is he?
Born Rozbih Khwushbudhan and trained as a Zoroastrian magus, this companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad converted to Islam after meeting him in Medina — who was he?

Salman the Persian: Companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Muhammad specifically said "Salman is part of my Ahl al-Bayt." In meetings with the other companions, he was often referred to by the kunya Abu ʿAbdullah.

For 17 years Carthage and Rome struggled for Mediterranean supremacy across Italy, Iberia, and North Africa, with Hannibal repeatedly crushing Roman legions before Carthage's eventual defeat — which of their three wars was this?
Second Punic War: War between Rome and Carthage (218–201 BC)
Founded in 1966 by Bal Thackeray as a Marathi nationalist, Hindutva-based movement, this Indian political party split into two rival factions in 2022 — what is it called?
Shiv Sena: Political party in Maharashtra, India.

Lasting from December 1979 to February 1989, this conflict saw mujahideen fighters — backed by Pakistan, the U.S. via Operation Cyclone, and others — battle a Communist superpower and its allied government. What war is it?
Soviet–Afghan War: 1979–1989 armed conflict in South Asia.
A London School of Economics graduate from a wealthy family, he led Togo from its 1958 election to independence as prime minister and then president, until his 1963 assassination — who was he?

Sylvanus Olympio: President of Togo from 1960 to 1963. After World War II, Olympio became prominent in efforts for independence of Togo and his party won the 1958 election, making him the prime minister of the country.
Formed in 2015 as a reformation of a party once led by Jacques Chirac, this conservative party, inspired by Gaullism, saw its 2017 presidential candidate place third — which party?
The only person to lead Labour to three consecutive general election victories, this MP for Sedgefield served as UK prime minister from 1997 to 2007 — who is he?
Tony Blair: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1997 to 2007.
This Portuguese nobleman opened the first direct sea route from Europe to India, rounding the Cape of Good Hope and crossing the Indian Ocean from Malindi in Kenya to Kozhikode. Who is he?
This Elizabethan explorer and statesman helped defend England against the Spanish Armada while also playing a leading role in colonizing North America — who was he?
Walter Raleigh: English statesman and explorer (1552–1618)

He started as a wildly successful Scottish privateer, commissioned by the governor of New York to hunt pirates and French ships in the Indian Ocean from his ship Adventure Galley — which sea captain, hanged in 1701, is it?
William Kidd: Scottish privateer (1654–1701). William Kidd (c. 1645 – 23 May 1701), also known as Captain William Kidd or simply Captain Kidd, was a Scottish privateer.
After defeating the last Zagwe king around 1270, this ruler founded Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty, which would endure until 1974 — who is he?
Yekuno Amlak: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1270 to 1285.
This French lawyer-turned-politician served as prime minister under Emmanuel Macron from 2017 to 2020, then returned to serve as mayor of Le Havre — who is he?
Édouard Philippe: Prime Minister of France from 2017 to 2020. A lawyer by occupation, Philippe is a former member of the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), which later became The Republicans (LR).
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four. Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 – October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four. C is a general-purpose programming language created in the 1970s by Dennis Ritchie.
Which of these was founded earliest?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
James Franck is a physicist. Franck became the head of the physics division of the Kaiser Wilhelm Gesellschaft for Physical Chemistry.
Who among these is a chemist?
Jack Parsons is a chemist. John Whiteside Parsons (born Marvel Whiteside Parsons; October 2, 1914 – June 17, 1952) was an American rocket engineer, chemist, and Thelemite occultist.
What is the atomic number of Fermium?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
In what year was Aryabhata born?
Aryabhata: The claim that Nalanda used to be located in Kusamapura/Pataliputra also cannot be proven.
In what year was Homi J. Bhabha born?
Homi J. Bhabha: Bhabha was awarded the Adams Prize (1942) and Padma Bhushan (1954), and nominated for the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1951 and 1953–1956.
In what year was Max Born?
Max Born: During World War I, Born was originally placed as a radio operator, but his specialist knowledge led to his being moved to research duties on sound ranging.
In what year did Katherine Johnson die?
Katherine Johnson: The space agency noted her "historical role as one of the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist".
In what year did Eratosthenes die?
Eratosthenes eventually became the chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria.
In what year was Caesium discovered?
Caesium (IUPAC spelling; also spelled cesium in American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
In what year was Osmium discovered?
Osmium (from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) 'smell') is a chemical element; it has symbol Os and atomic number 76.
Which company manufactures AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo?
AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo: Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation. The aircraft made its first flight in 1989.
In which country is Virgo interferometer?
Virgo interferometer: Italy. The Virgo interferometer is a large-scale scientific instrument near Pisa, Italy, for detecting gravitational waves.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
First described by Othniel C. Marsh in 1877, this late Jurassic theropod's name means 'different lizard,' a nod to its unusually lightweight vertebrae — what dinosaur is it?
Allosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived 155 to 143 million years ago during the late Jurassic period (latest Oxfordian to latest Tithonian ages).
This symptom, not a diagnosis by itself, refers to a loss of appetite in humans and — under the name 'inappetence' — in animals from dogs to goats. Which symptom?
Anorexia (symptom) is a medical term for a loss of appetite.
This medical condition, most often caused in the developed world by liver cirrhosis, is the abnormal buildup of fluid within the abdominal cavity — what is it called?
Ascites is the abnormal build-up of fluid in the abdomen.

Ranking among the largest wild cats, this population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies has roamed the Indian subcontinent since the Late Pleistocene and is found from India to southwestern China — name it?
Bengal tiger is a population of the Panthera tigris tigris subspecies. It is distributed from India, southern Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan to Southwestern China.
This rigid, mineralized organ of the vertebrate skeleton produces both red and white blood cells and helps regulate the body's acid-base balance — what is it?
Bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals.
This soft, silvery-white metal shares group 12 of the periodic table with zinc and mercury, resembling zinc in its chemistry and mercury in its low melting point — what element, symbol Cd, is it?
Cadmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cd and atomic number 48.
This neuropsychiatric syndrome, often linked to mood or psychotic disorders, can leave a person nearly motionless for days or cause repetitive, purposeless movements. What is it?
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome most commonly seen in people with underlying mood disorders such as major depressive disorder, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
Native to East Asia and blooming late in the season, these autumn flowers of the daisy family are associated in the Northern Hemisphere with the month of November. What flower is it?
Chrysanthemum (kriss-), sometimes abbreviated to mums or chrysanths, are perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that bloom in the autumn.
This highly poisonous member of the carrot family can grow to nearly 8 feet tall, with hollow, maroon-spotted stems and a famously unpleasant odor — what plant is it?
Conium maculatum (British English) or poison hemlock (in North America), is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.
This Zambian-born economist turned four of her five books into New York Times bestsellers, including a provocative argument that foreign aid actually holds Africa back — who is she?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo (born 2 February 1969) is a Zambian-born economist and author, known for her analysis of macroeconomics and global affairs.
This Canadian optical physicist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing chirped pulse amplification, a breakthrough in pulsed lasers. Who is she?
Donna Strickland (born May 27, 1959) is a Canadian optical physicist and pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers.

This German chess champion — also a mathematician and philosopher — held the world title for 27 years, the longest reign ever, and was famed for a 'psychological' approach said to unsettle opponents. Who was he?
Emanuel Lasker (German; December 24, 1868 - January 11, 1941) was a German chess player, mathematician, and philosopher.
Distinct from secretion, this bodily process includes exhaling carbon dioxide, sweating, and passing urine through the bladder and urethra — what's it called?
Excretion is elimination of metabolic waste, which is an essential process in all organisms.
This American physician-scientist discovered genes tied to several diseases, led the Human Genome Project, and went on to direct the NIH under three presidents — who is he?
Francis Collins (born April 14, 1950) is an American physician-scientist who discovered the genes associated with a number of diseases and led the Human Genome Project.
This flowering plant genus, whose name derives from the Latin word for a small sword, belongs to the iris family and is centered on the Cape Floristic Region of South Africa — which genus?
Gladiolus (from Latin, the diminutive of gladius, a sword) is a genus of perennial cormous flowering plants in the iris family (Iridaceae).
This flatfish's English name blends words for 'holy' and 'flat fish,' a nod to its place on the Catholic holy-day menu. Which bottom-dwelling fish?
Halibut is the common name for three species of flatfish in the family of right-eye flounders.
Before founding his own Italian supercar company, this Argentine-Italian engineer worked for both Renault and Lamborghini — who is he?
Horacio Pagani (auto executive) (born 10 November 1955) is an Argentine-Italian businessman and automobile engineer in the automotive industry.
Its partial form is called 'subileus' — this condition describes an intestine that can't propel its contents forward, whether from a lack of peristalsis or a mechanical blockage — what is it?
Ileus is a disruption of the normal propulsive ability of the intestine.
This NASA astronaut and Marine Corps test pilot commanded the SpaceX Crew-7 mission and served as a flight engineer aboard the International Space Station — who is she?
Jasmin Moghbeli (born June 24, 1983) is an American U.S.
Brewed from the root of a Pacific pepper plant and sipped from a communal bowl in island ceremonies, this psychoactive drink takes its bitter-tasting name from Tongan and Marquesan — what is it?
Kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
Representing the Nemean Lion slain by Heracles as one of his twelve labors, this zodiac constellation sits between Cancer and Virgo — which constellation?
Leo (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac, between Cancer, the Crab, to the west and Virgo, the Maiden, to the east.
This Berkeley professor upended classical logic by proposing 'fuzzy' mathematics — fuzzy sets, fuzzy logic, fuzzy control, and more — who was he?

Lotfi A. Zadeh (4 February 1921 - 6 September 2017) was a mathematician, computer scientist, electrical engineer, artificial intelligence researcher, and professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley.

This Milanese thinker was the first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed a mathematics professor — though she spent her final decades on theology and serving the poor. Who was she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi (16 May 1718 - 9 January 1799) was a Milanese mathematician, philosopher, theologian, and humanitarian.
This hedge fund manager and licensed physician was among the first to predict and profit from the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, later portrayed on screen in The Big Short. Who is he?
Michael Burry (born June 19, 1971) is an American investor, hedge fund manager, and licensed physician.
This Turkish government minister for environment and climate will preside over the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference, COP31 — who is he?
Murat Kurum is the minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change in Turkey, and president of the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31.

A former director of Russia's FSB intelligence agency, this politician served as Secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024 and is considered one of Putin's closest advisors — who is he?
Nikolai Patrushev (born 11 July 1951) is a Russian politician, security officer and former intelligence officer who served as the secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024.
Chemists still debate the exact definition, but generally, any large molecule containing a carbon-hydrogen or carbon-carbon bond falls into this broad class of compounds. What is it?
Organic compound are a subclass of chemical compounds of carbon.
This pulse crop, given the scientific name Pisum sativum by Linnaeus in 1753, is usually eaten as a vegetable via its small round seeds. What is it?
Pea is a pulse or fodder crop, but the word often refers to the seed or sometimes the pod of this flowering plant species.
Odorless when pure but reeking of rotting fish in technical grade, this colorless PH3 gas can burst into a luminous flame on contact with air — what highly toxic compound is it?
Phosphine (IUPAC name: phosphane) is a colorless, flammable, highly toxic compound with the chemical formula PH3, classed as a pnictogen hydride.

Attacks of this condition — abdominal pain, vomiting, and confusion lasting days to weeks — stem from a buildup of porphyrins and can be triggered by stress, smoking, or certain medications. What is it?
Porphyria (or) is a group of disorders in which substances called porphyrins build up in the body, adversely affecting the skin or nervous system.
Found in nucleic acids as the building block behind adenine and guanine, this nitrogen-rich heterocyclic compound is the most common of its kind in nature — what is it?
Purine is a heterocyclic aromatic organic compound that consists of two rings (pyrimidine and imidazole) fused together.

One of the rarest and most valuable precious metals, this hard, corrosion-resistant transition metal with only one naturally occurring isotope is prized for enhancing jewelry — what's the element (symbol Rh, atomic number 45)?
Rhodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rh and atomic number 45.
Having taught economics at the Catholic University of Asunción and once served as Paraguay's finance minister, this politician assumed his country's presidency in 2023 — who is he?
Santiago Peña (Spanish; born 16 November 1978) is a Paraguayan politician and economist who has served as the 52nd president of Paraguay since 2023.

Dubbed the "father of modern differential geometry," this Chinese-born American mathematician and poet won the Wolf Prize — and has a medal named for him by the International Mathematical Union. Who was he?
Shiing-Shen Chern (pinyin: Chn Xngshn; October 26, 1911 - December 3, 2004) was a Chinese-born American mathematician and poet.

Meaning 'pore bearer' in Greek, this phylum of sessile, filter-feeding marine invertebrates has tube-like bodies of jelly-like material sandwiched between thin cell layers, letting water circulate through countless pores — name the animal group?
Sponge are primarily marine invertebrates of the animal phylum Porifera (meaning 'pore bearer').
This South African biologist established the tiny roundworm C. elegans as a model organism, work that helped earn him a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Who was he?
Sydney Brenner (13 January 1927 - 5 April 2019) was a South African biologist.
Raised in Michigan with little schooling, he sold his first inventions by age 22 and moved to New York to chase engineering — going on to become one of America's most famous inventors. Who?
Thomas Edison (February 11, 1847 - October 18, 1931) was an American inventor and businessman.
Caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis and treated with the antibiotic streptomycin, this tick-borne illness also goes by an animal-related nickname — what is it?
Tularemia is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis.
This Russian-American inventor built a television system using cathode-ray tubes and worked on image tubes and the electron microscope — who was he?
Vladimir K. Zworykin (1888/1889 - July 29, 1982) was a Russian-American inventor, engineer, and pioneer of television technology.
The first woman ever to serve as Ukraine's prime minister, this politician held that post in 2005 and again from 2007 to 2010, and now leads the Batkivshchyna political party — who is she?

Yulia Tymoshenko (ne Hrihyan; born 27 November 1960) is a Ukrainian politician, who served as Prime Minister of Ukraine in 2005, and again from 2007 until 2010; the first woman in Ukraine to hold that position.
Nicknamed the 'upside-down tree' for its unusual silhouette, this genus of long-lived African and Malagasy giants was named after a French naturalist — what genus is it?
Adansonia: Genus of trees known as baobab.
Made in the adrenal cortex, this hormone tells the kidney to hang onto sodium and dump potassium, quietly steering your blood pressure and blood volume — what is it?
A colourless gas of nitrogen and hydrogen with a famously pungent smell, this compound has about 70% of its industrial output turned into fertilisers — what is it?
Ammonia: Chemical compound. A stable binary hydride and the simplest pnictogen hydride, ammonia is a colourless gas with a distinctive pungent smell.
Born Fernando Martins de Bulhões, this 13th-century Portuguese Catholic priest joined the Order of Friars Minor — who is he?
Anthony of Padua: Portuguese Catholic saint (1195–1231)
A notoriously toxic metalloid and pnictogen with atomic number 33, it's used in lead alloys for car batteries and ammunition and as a semiconductor dopant — which element is it?
Arsenic: Chemical element with atomic number 33 (As). It is a metalloid and one of the pnictogens, and therefore shares many properties with its group 15 neighbors phosphorus and antimony.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
A colorless, sweet-smelling liquid hiding in petroleum, this ring-shaped hydrocarbon helps give gasoline its distinctive aroma — what is it?
Composed of plasma plus red cells, white cells, and platelets, this circulatory fluid delivers oxygen and nutrients to the body while carrying away waste — what is it?
Blood: Body fluid in the circulatory system. Plasma, which constitutes 55% of blood fluid, is mostly water (92% by volume), and contains proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones.
This plant family — nicknamed the mustards or crucifers, and including cabbage — hosts the caterpillars of a notorious garden-pest butterfly as one of its worst enemies — name the family?

Ranging from the hefty black species of the Amazon basin to the diminutive dwarf species just over a metre long, these Central and South American relatives of alligators make up their own reptile subfamily — what are they called?
Caiman: Subfamily of reptiles. The black caiman is the largest caiman species in the world and is found in the slow-moving rivers and lakes that surround the Amazon basin.

Born in London, raised in Milan, and self-taught in web design, this Catholic teenager built a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles before dying of leukemia at fifteen — he was beatified in 2020. Who was he?
Which second-generation antihistamine for hay fever kicks in within half an hour but is more likely than fexofenadine or loratadine to cause drowsiness?

Cetirizine: Antihistamine medication. Cetirizine is a second-generation peripherally selective antihistamine used to treat allergic rhinitis (hay fever), dermatitis, urticaria (hives), and runny nose.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Believed to be the first coffee species ever cultivated, this plant, native to the forests of Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Yemen, still accounts for roughly 60% of global coffee production — what's its scientific name?
Coffea arabica: Species of coffee plant. Coffea arabica, also known as the Arabica coffee, is a species of flowering plant in the coffee and madder family Rubiaceae.
Found only in placental mammals, this roughly four-inch bundle of 200 to 300 million nerve fibers is the brain's largest white-matter structure, linking its left and right hemispheres — what is it?
Corpus callosum: White matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, this disorder coats the lungs and other organs in thick mucus, inviting repeated bacterial infections — what genetic condition is it?
Cystic fibrosis: Genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.

Aristotle's Poetics contrasted this performance-based mode with the epic and the lyrical, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "deed" or "act" — the two-masks symbol marks its split into comedy and tragedy. What is it?
Drama: Artwork intended for performance; formal type of literature.
The largest living land animal comes in three recognized species and counts mammoths and mastodons among its extinct cousins — what is it?
Elephant: Largest living land animal. The trunk is prehensile, bringing food and water to the mouth and grasping objects.
Marketed as Lexapro, this SSRI treats depression and anxiety but is exclusively sold commercially as an oxalate salt — what is it?

Escitalopram: SSRI antidepressant. It is mainly used to treat major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), and social anxiety disorder.
With a black-tipped bushy tail and brownish-grey striped fur, this small wild feline lives in Scotland, Turkey, the Caucasus, and mainland forests, hunting rodents and ground birds — which species?
European wildcat: Small wild cat. The European wildcat (Felis silvestris) is a small wildcat species that was described in the late 18th century.
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
This cold-weather injury turns skin white or waxy-blue after tissue actually freezes, often preceded by a tingling, numb warning stage called frostnip — what is it?
Frostbite: Effect of low temperature on skin and other tissues.
First described by J. D. Hooker in 1889 and nicknamed the Transvaal or Barberton daisy for its South African origins, what genus of flowering plant is this?
Gerbera: Genus of plants. Gerbera ( JUR-bər-ə or GUR-bər-ə) L. is a genus of plants in the Asteraceae (Compositae) family.
This system of rules governing clauses, phrases, and word use is often absorbed unconsciously in childhood, long before anyone studies its syntax formally — what field?
Grammar: Structural rules of a language.

Marketed under a well-known brand name, this typical antipsychotic treats everything from schizophrenia to Tourette tics, but carries risks of tardive dyskinesia and dangerous QT-interval prolongation — what drug is it?
Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic medication. Haloperidol, sold under the brand name Haldol among others, is a typical antipsychotic medication.

Synthesized from the dried latex of the opium poppy, this opioid is used medically in some countries to relieve pain during childbirth or a heart attack — and its 'black tar' form is a crude, variable mix of morphine derivatives — what is it?
Heroin: Opioid analgesic and recreational drug.
The flowers of this shrub genus act as natural pH indicators, turning blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil?
Powered by four underperforming Lyulka turbojets, this aircraft became the first Soviet jet bomber to fly before being cancelled in September 1947 — which plane?
Ilyushin Il-22: 1947 Soviet bomber aircraft prototype. The Ilyushin Il-22, USAF/DOD designation Type 10, was the first Soviet jet-engined bomber to fly.
As president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995, this French politician spearheaded the creation of the single market and laid the groundwork for the euro — who is he?
A real estate magnate and Spanish–American War officer worth roughly $87 million, he was the richest passenger aboard the Titanic — and went down with it in 1912. Who was he?
John Jacob Astor IV: American businessman and Titanic passenger (1864–1912)
This German-Finnish internet entrepreneur founded the file-hosting service Megaupload before U.S. authorities seized it in 2012 — who is he?

This trigonometric relationship links each side of a triangle to the angle across from it, with every such ratio equal to twice the radius of the triangle's circumscribed circle. What is the rule called?
Law of sines: Property of all triangles on a Euclidean plane.
Patented in 1978 and approved for use in the US in 1987, this ACE inhibitor is a common first-line treatment for high blood pressure — what drug is it?
Lisinopril: Medication used to treat hypertension and heart failure.
This American biologist argued that cells with nuclei arose from symbiotic mergers of bacteria, and co-developed the Gaia hypothesis with James Lovelock — who was she?

Raising silkworms at 13 and publishing a two-volume study of caterpillars, this German-Dutch artist was among the earliest European naturalists to document insects from direct observation — who was she?
Maria Sibylla Merian: German naturalist and artist (1647–1717)
Comprising 18 to 24 species that hybridize freely where their ranges overlap, this genus of the mint family thrives in wet, moist soils worldwide — what is it?
Mentha: Genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae.
Based on a Soviet fighter jet but optimized for ground attack, this variable-sweep aircraft was license-built in India as the 'Bahadur,' or 'Valiant' — which jet?
Mikoyan MiG-27: Series of 1970s Soviet attack aircraft.
Grown to feed silkworms for commercial silk production, this fast-growing tree releases its pollen at more than half the speed of sound — which species?
Morus alba: Plant species in the fig family.

The males of this stocky Arctic cetacean sport a spiralled 'tusk' up to three metres long — actually a protruding left canine tooth thought to work as a weapon, a tool, and maybe a salinity sensor. What animal is it?

Usually made from unleavened dough that's rolled, cut, or extruded into long strips, this staple food is called pasta in Italian cuisine and split into wheat-based and starch-based varieties in Chinese cooking — what is it?
Noodle: Staple food made from unleavened dough, commonly long and thin.

Born out of military planning before World War II, this branch of applied mathematics uses optimization and statistics to find the best possible outcome for real-world decisions — what field, sometimes called management science?
Operations research: Discipline concerning the application of advanced analytical methods.
Also called the corn poppy or Flanders poppy, this red flowering weed has symbolized remembrance in the Commonwealth since World War I — what plant is it?
Papaver rhoeas: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family.
Native to Asia, Europe, and western North America, this flowering shrub's fragrant blooms last just 7 to 10 days each spring — which plant?
Peony: Genus of flowering plants in the family Paeoniaceae.
Known across South Asia as Indian gooseberry or amla, this deciduous tree is native to tropical regions of the continent — which plant?
Phyllanthus emblica: Berry and plant. Phyllanthus emblica, commonly known as emblic, Indian gooseberry, amalaki, amloki, or amla, is a deciduous tree of the family Phyllanthaceae.
This birth defect results in one or more extra fingers or toes and has been linked to at least 39 different genetic mutations — what is it called?
Polydactyly: Physical anomaly involving extra fingers or toes.

Native to western Eurasia and a member of the rose family, this species — the wild or sweet cherry — is the ancestor of the sour cherry, though every part of the plant except its ripe fruit is mildly toxic. What is it called?
Prunus avium: Species of flowering plant in the rose family. The species is often cultivated as an ornamental tree.
Also known as hexogen, this nitroamine explosive is the key energetic agent in C-4 and a core ingredient of Semtex — which compound?
RDX: Explosive chemical compound. RDX (Research Department Explosive or Royal Demolition Explosive), or hexogen, also known by other names, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2N2O2)3.

Covering more than 200 conditions from arthritis to soft-tissue pain syndromes, this umbrella term for chronic joint and connective-tissue pain gives its name to a whole medical specialty — what is it called?
Rheumatism: Medical conditions affecting the joints or connective tissue.
Known as rue or 'herb-of-grace,' this Mediterranean plant is prized for its bluish leaves and doubles as an insect repellent — which species?
Ruta graveolens: Species of plant. Ruta graveolens, commonly known as rue, common rue, ruda, arruda or herb-of-grace, is a species of the genus Ruta grown as an ornamental plant and herb.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers and toes, with one form known as CREST syndrome — what is it called?
Scleroderma: Group of autoimmune diseases resulting in abnormal growth of connective tissue.
Also called herpes zoster, this viral disease paints a painful blistering rash down just one side of the body, and can leave lingering nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia — what is it?
Shingles: Viral disease caused by the varicella zoster virus.

Pernod Ricard: French company that produces distilled beverages.

Smith & Wesson: American manufacturer of firearms and ammunition.

Walmart: American multinational retail corporation operating department stores.
